candidates.mechanism: Per description and post preview: treat project information like code so agents work from current decisions; give the next stretch of work a defined output; diagnose drift with a four-row table of causes (worked on a proposal draft that copied the wrong price); team-level shared skills, roles/permissions in a shared repo, collision avoidance between agents. candidates.worth_watching: 03:27 Getting the right context in front of the AI; 05:14 Treat project information like code; 10:57 Roles and permissions in a shared repo; 12:53 Avoiding collisions when agents share work; 17:28 Start alone with one job you keep explaining.
candidates.summary: Nate argues that whether an overnight agent run saves or costs a day depends on the structure around it, not a smarter model. He opens with a personal research run that went sideways because the assignment, not the data, was wrong, then walks through: getting the right context in front of the model, keeping project decisions versioned like code so agents don't revert to stale plans, building skills for the team rather than for one person, roles and permissions in a shared repo, avoiding collisions when several agents touch the same work, and how to judge whether it's working. He closes with advice to start alone with one job you keep re-explaining. The Substack post (paid) adds a four-cause diagnosis table and a 'Long-Running Work Companion' with examples, worksheets and five prompts; only the free preview was readable.

candidates.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
candidates.author: OpenAI
candidates.what_changed: OpenAI describes defenses against extraction of protected reasoning; with GPT-6.2 Astra/Sol, protected reasoning is tied to the conversation history that produced it.
candidates.mechanism: Adversarial training, input/output classifiers (including tool-call arguments), API-level restrictions on reusing encrypted reasoning across user/workspace/org/model-family boundaries, campaign-level detection. Internal adaptive eval: reasoning-extraction attack success fell from 54.0% (GPT-6 Astra, original safeguards) to 0.2% (GPT-6.2 Astra). Internal study: students trained on exact reasoning traces gained more cyber capability than those trained on summaries.
candidates.relevance: medium for API builders who pass encrypted reasoning between calls/conversations
candidates.summary: Practical implication for developers: reasoning artifacts from GPT-6.2 are bound to their originating conversation and boundaries; reuse across conversations/orgs is restricted.
